articles.title: SMS frauduleux : les bons réflexes pour signaler, se protéger et sécuriser ses données
articles.text:
Comment signaler un SMS frauduleux et protéger son téléphone
Faux colis, fausse alerte bancaire, remboursement suspect : voici comment reconnaître un SMS frauduleux, le signaler au 33700 et protéger votre téléphone.
Un faux avis de livraison qui réclame un paiement, une alerte bancaire alarmante, un remboursement inattendu ou une menace de compte bloqué : ces SMS frauduleux envahissent chaque jour un peu plus les téléphones en France.
Derrière ce spam sms se cache presque toujours la même logique, pousser l'utilisateur à cliquer sur un lien, saisir ses identifiants ou installer une application douteuse. Le phénomène ne se limite d'ailleurs pas au SMS classique : un mail frauduleux, un courriel imitant un service connu ou un appel indésirable poursuivent exactement le même objectif, avec des scénarios qui évoluent sans cesse au gré de l'actualité, période de fêtes, soldes, ou nouvelles réglementations administratives. Reconnaître ces messages, savoir les signaler et adopter les bons réflexes après réception, voilà l'objectif de ce dossier.
Le top 4 des solutions de sécurité
Comment signaler un SMS frauduleux au 33700 ?
En France, la procédure officielle est simple et gratuite : il suffit de transférer le SMS suspect par un simple message au numéro 33700, le service national de signalement des spams sms et des appels indésirables. Il est également possible de signaler un message via la plateforme officielle 33700, en y joignant une capture d'écran du SMS reçu ainsi que, si possible, le numéro de téléphone de l'expéditeur.
Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr indique que ce signalement permet de faire bloquer l'émetteur du message et contribue à l'effort collectif de lutte contre le phishing et les appels frauduleux. Ce geste, qui prend quelques secondes, alimente une base de données utilisée pour repérer les campagnes les plus actives et pour signaler les numéros frauduleux aux opérateurs. Plus les utilisateurs sont nombreux à signaler ces messages, plus le dispositif devient efficace pour identifier rapidement une nouvelle vague de sms frauduleux.
La même logique de signalement s'applique d'ailleurs à un mail frauduleux : signaler un courriel suspect auprès du service concerné participe à la même dynamique de protection collective, que la menace arrive par sms, mms ou messagerie électronique.
Comment reconnaître un SMS frauduleux ?
Le premier signal d'alerte, c'est souvent l'urgence. Un message qui exige une action immédiate, sous peine de suspension de service ou de blocage de compte, doit systématiquement éveiller la méfiance. Les fautes d'orthographe étranges, une formulation maladroite ou un ton inhabituel par rapport aux communications habituelles d'un service client constituent un deuxième indice révélateur. La mise en forme peut également trahir la supercherie : logo pixelisé, absence de mentions légales habituelles, ou signature générique plutôt que personnalisée.
Le lien raccourci, difficile à vérifier avant de cliquer, est une autre caractéristique typique du hameçonnage par SMS. Un numéro inconnu, parfois surtaxé, une demande de paiement présentée comme urgente, une menace de suspension de service, ou à l'inverse une promesse de remboursement inespérée, tout cela doit alerter. Ces techniques, proches de celles utilisées par courriel, exploitent la même mécanique de pression psychologique, qu'il s'agisse d'un SMS, d'un MMS ou d'un message reçu sur une messagerie classique.
Autre point de vigilance : l'expéditeur affiché n'est pas toujours fiable. Un message peut sembler provenir d'un service client légitime alors que le numéro de téléphone réel appartient à un tout autre expéditeur. Comparer les coordonnées du service client affichées dans le message avec celles communiquées officiellement par l'entreprise reste l'un des moyens les plus simples de démasquer une tentative d'hameçonnage.
Que faire après avoir reçu un SMS suspect ?
La règle d’or, c’est de ne jamais cliquer sur le lien, même juste pour voir. Ne répondez pas non plus au SMS et ne rappelez pas le numéro : cela montre aux escrocs que votre ligne est active, et vous recevrez encore plus d'arnaques. Prenez plutôt une capture d’écran pour garder une preuve, puis signalez le message et bloquez le numéro dans les paramètres de votre téléphone.
Le site Cybermalveillance.gouv.fr insiste aussi sur un point : n'installez jamais d'application en dehors des magasins officiels (comme Google Play ou l'App Store) après avoir cliqué sur un lien louche. Ces applications cachées servent souvent à vider vos comptes ou à voler vos données.
Ce réflexe tout simple suffit pour bloquer la plupart des arnaques. Si vous avez encore un doute, passez plutôt par le site officiel de l'entreprise concernée pour trouver ses vraies coordonnées. N'utilisez jamais celles fournies dans le SMS.
Que faire si vous avez cliqué sur le lien ?
Si le lien a déjà été ouvert, ou pire, si des informations ont été saisies sur la page frauduleuse, plusieurs actions s'imposent rapidement. Il faut d'abord changer ses mots de passe sur l'ensemble des services concernés, en particulier ceux des sites bancaires et des comptes associés à des données personnelles sensibles. Changez également les identifiants réutilisés sur d'autres services, une pratique encore répandue mais risquée dès qu'un mot de passe a pu être compromis. Si des coordonnées bancaires ont été renseignées, contacter sans attendre le service client de sa banque permet de faire opposition ou de surveiller les mouvements suspects sur le compte.
Il est également conseillé de surveiller ses comptes dans les jours qui suivent, de supprimer toute application installée depuis la page frauduleuse, et de lancer une analyse de sécurité complète du téléphone. Ces étapes, appliquées sans délai, limitent fortement l'impact d'un clic malheureux et évitent qu'une simple erreur ne se transforme en vol de données personnelles à grande échelle.
Un antivirus peut-il protéger contre les SMS frauduleux ?
Il faut être clair sur ce point : aucun antivirus ne remplace le signalement au 33700, qui reste le seul canal officiel capable de faire bloquer un numéro frauduleux à la source. En revanche, une solution de sécurité installée sur le téléphone joue un rôle complémentaire précieux.
Des applications reconnues comme Avast, Norton 360, Surfshark, Bitdefender Mobile Security ou Malwarebytes peuvent bloquer l'accès à une page de phishing avant même que l'utilisateur n'ait eu le temps de saisir la moindre information.
Ces outils permettent également de détecter une application malveillante installée par erreur et d'analyser les fichiers téléchargés après un clic malencontreux sur un lien douteux. Certaines solutions incluent aussi un filtre dédié capable de bloquer les notifications d'appels ou de messages suspects, complétant ainsi le service de signalement des spams proposé par les opérateurs.
Pour un usage quotidien du téléphone, entre messages professionnels, notifications bancaires et échanges personnels, cette double protection, le réflexe de signalement d'un côté et une solution de sécurité active de l'autre, forme la meilleure défense contre la multiplication des sms frauduleux et des appels indésirables.
Un geste de vigilance à chaque message reçu, associé à un outil qui veille en arrière-plan, permet de garder le contrôle sur ses données et ses services sans jamais céder à la panique face à un message alarmant. Avec le temps, ces réflexes deviennent presque automatiques, un peu comme on vérifie la provenance d'un colis avant de l'ouvrir. Comment signaler, quand agir, comment réagir après un clic : ces trois réflexes, une fois acquis, suffisent à transformer la méfiance en simple routine de sécurité.

articles.title: EU will require companies to label AI-generated content starting Sunday
articles.text:
The takeaway: Companies operating in the European Union are now subject to a new requirement: clearly label content created or altered by artificial intelligence. Beginning Sunday, the EU's latest transparency rules take effect, covering everything from chatbot responses to AI-generated images, audio, and video. The aim is simple: users should be able to tell, without guessing, whether what they are seeing or hearing is real or machine-generated.
The rule is part of the EU's broader artificial intelligence law, which is being rolled out in phases. This first step focuses on disclosure. If content is generated by AI or significantly manipulated by it, companies must make that clear. That includes adding visible labels as well as technical markers, such as watermarks or embedded metadata, that help identify synthetic material.
The push comes as deepfakes and other AI-generated media become more convincing and easier to produce. Regulators are particularly concerned about how quickly this content can spread and how difficult it has become to determine what is real.
The requirements apply mainly to content created in professional contexts. Material designed to inform the public about matters of general interest must carry a label if it is produced by AI without human editorial oversight. At the same time, the EU has carved out exceptions. Individuals using AI for personal purposes are not covered, and exemptions exist for "artistic, creative, satirical, fictional" works.
From a technical standpoint, the rules go beyond simple on-screen labels. Companies are expected to implement systems that can identify AI-generated content even after it has been shared or reposted. That means relying on watermarking and tagging tools that can persist across platforms.
Major tech companies have already been moving in this direction. TikTok, for example, has required creators to label AI-generated content for several years and says more than three billion pieces of content have been tagged using its detection tools. Meta has introduced an "AI Info" label on Facebook and Instagram to flag posts created with generative AI technology.
Google has signed on to the EU's voluntary code of conduct on AI transparency and is working with companies including Nvidia, OpenAI, and Apple on digital tagging standards designed to track content origins.
Still, not everyone is convinced the rollout will be smooth. Some companies argue that the rules add another layer of complexity to already crowded platforms.
Karen Massin of Google said the added regulatory complexity could end up being counterproductive and warned that it may confuse the very users the rules are intended to help.
The concern is that if users are constantly seeing labels and disclosures, those signals may lose their meaning. Too many overlapping indicators could make it harder, not easier, for people to understand what they are looking at.
Even so, others see the situation as familiar territory. Compliance requirements often face pushback early on but eventually become standard practice.
"We have heard that it is going to be very, very difficult to implement. But I think we often hear this with compliance requirements. And yet, the world turns and we figure these things out," Ashley Casovan of the International Association of Privacy Professionals told AFP.
Companies have until December 2 to bring existing AI systems into compliance. After that, enforcement will tighten, with significant fines for those that fail to meet the requirements.

articles.title: Opus 5 vs. Fable 5: What does half the price buy?
articles.text:
Opus 5 vs. Fable 5: What does half the price buy?
Anthropic released Claude Opus 5 last week, with this pitch: It comes “close to the frontier intelligence of Claude Fable 5 at half the price.”
Opus 5 runs $5 per million input tokens and $25 per million output tokens, unchanged from Opus 4.8. Meanwhile, Fable 5 runs $10 and $50. It also became the default model on Claude Max, which means a lot of people started using it whether they noticed or not.
Anthropic compared the two and reported Opus 5 winning eight of them. It also published a sentence that most of the launch coverage skipped past. “Claude Opus 5 is not more capable overall than our most capable general-access model, Claude Fable 5.”
I was confused. Is Opus 5 better, cheaper, or the same as Fable 5? I had to get to the bottom of this, so I ran all reasoning-based tasks. Since differences between the two models seem hard to identify, I decided to test reasoning tasks because, in my opinion, those are the hardest tasks for AI models to complete successfully.
| Benchmark | Opus 5 | Fable 5 | Opus 4.8 | GPT-5.6 Sol | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Agentic terminal coding Frontier-Bench v0.1 | 43.3% | 33.7% | 18.7% | 37.5% | 
| Knowledge work GDPval-AA v2 | 1861 | 1747 | 1593 | 1736 | 
| Agentic search BrowseComp | 90.8% | 87.4% | 84.3% | 90.4% | 
| Multidisciplinary reasoning Humanity’s Last Exam | 56.3% no tools 64.7% with tools | 56.5% no tools 63.9% with tools | 49.8% no tools 57.9% with tools | — — | 
| Computer use OSWorld 2.0 | 70.6% | 66.1% | 55.7% | 62.6% | 
| Agentic coding DeepSWE v1.1 | 68.8% | 69.7% | 59.0% | 72.7% | 
| Agentic coding FrontierCode v1.1, Main | 53.4% | 53.5% | 46.5% | 47.5% | 
| Business workflows AutomationBench | 26.0% | 17.4% | 17.0% | 18.1% | 
| Legal Legal Agent Benchmark, Held-out | 11.7% | 13.3% | 10.4% | 2.5% | 
| Health HealthBench Professional | 59.8% | Mythos 5 66.0% | 57.4% | 60.5% | 
| Biology BioMysteryBench | 49.4% hard 90.1% human solved | 46.5% hard Mythos 5 89.0% human solved | 42.4% hard 88.5% human solved | — — | 
The tests
I used the same prompts, fresh terminal sessions, and made sure there was no cross-contamination between models. Here are the three tests I ran (in this order):
- A diagnosis-only bug hunt on a live open source bug
- An analytics job on a financial statement I rigged with 27 planted errors
- A synthesis memo on conflicting claims in AI marketing
For every test, I recorded API time, output tokens, and cost from the /cost command in Claude Code.
Test one: diagnosis-only bug hunt
Test one was a diagnosis-only bug hunt (I asked the models not to code anything). I used Hypothesis, the Python property-based testing library, and checked out version 6.130.10 where a real assertion bug was still live (issue #4339). The bug causes a user’s test to crash with an internal assertion, which is a check Hypothesis runs on itself, so the user’s test crashes inside library code they never wrote. The bug is so nuanced that two maintainers couldn’t reproduce it themselves.
I gave each model the traceback and the reproducer and told it to work from the codebase with no web access and no code changes. The maintainers’ real fix shipped in PR #4349, so I had something to measure the models’ responses against.
Both models found the same root cause. It was a strategy built inside a composite that gets rebuilt on every test run and labeled by its memory address. The same value gets two different labels across two runs. A cleanup step compares those labels and crashes when they do not match.
Both proposed the maintainers’ fix. Fable suggested it as its first-choice fix. Opus listed it second, behind a different approach targeting the same cause one step earlier. There were two main differences in the models’ responses.
Only Fable explained the intermittency of the bug and why it was so challenging for maintainers to reproduce. Only Opus wrote code, monkeypatching a fix in memory and running the suite against it despite being told not to modify anything.
Opus finished in 14 minutes 13 seconds of API time on 58.6K output tokens for $4.90. Fable took 18 minutes 18 seconds on 68.5K tokens for $8.97.
Both models satisfied the prompt’s requirement of identifying the root cause. Fable went one step further and explained why the bug only shows up sometimes, but Opus went ahead and tested the fix. Fable wins reasoning. Opus wins attention to detail.
Test two: the rigged spreadsheet
Test two was built to mirror a test I did on Claude for Small Business earlier this summer. I created a fake B2B SaaS company and built a financial statement that included seven months of numbers across eleven tabs and twenty customers.
Then I planted 27 problems ranked easy, medium, and hard. Easy problems are obvious, like a customer billed the month after they churned. Hard problems need three facts chained across separate tabs to identify. I also planted three red herrings, things that look like problems and aren’t, so that I could count false positives.
What they did right
Both caught every hard problem I expected them to miss. They spotted the same customer entered twice under slightly different names, because the usage rows were identical to the last digit. They caught the partner account booked at full price when the notes and the invoice both say net. Both flagged the euro contract summed into dollars at one to one, and the retention table claiming nobody churned from a group that lost a customer. Neither missed the CAC number divided by trial starts instead of conversions.
Fable went one step further than Opus when it came to reasoning over the data. It rebuilt the monthly revenue numbers as they should have been reported, which showed a business that was flat to shrinking rather than growing. It then noticed that every error it found worked in the business’s favor. Fable explained this by saying, “every distortion in the reported numbers happens to flatter the business.”
Where it went wrong
Both models missed a Simpson’s paradox in the trials funnel. That’s where self-serve trials convert at around 13% and sales-assisted at around 45%, and both rates improved over the seven months, but self-serve grew as a share of the total, so the blended rate fell from 22.5% to 16.9%. The headline says conversion is getting worse. Both channels say it is getting better.
Fable also missed a customer billed $449 against a $499 list price and flagged one downgrade without noticing the second. Both are small, checkable numbers sitting in a single tab. Neither one required the kind of thinking Fable had already proven it could do.
Opus cost $0.98 on 4 minutes 59 seconds of API time and 22.8K output tokens. Fable cost $1.76 in 4 minutes 36 seconds and 20.3K tokens.
The results of this test repeat the pattern from test one. Opus found 26 of the 27; Fable found 24. Fable is stronger when it comes to “thought” and reasoning; Opus is stronger on attention to detail.
This test also reconfirmed the same thing as the original test: You still need an expert to review financial data.
Test three: models recommending models
Test three focused on my favorite topic, conflicting claims in AI marketing. I saved four files from this month’s launches, two vendor announcements, plus Artificial Analysis measurements and five aggregators. Every independent number in this test came from Artificial Analysis. I found 16 contradictions and asked Opus and Fable which model a developer should run. Or, to put it in other terms, can AI replace my job?
TL;DR: No.
Opus caught 15 of the conflicting claims, and Fable caught 12. I’m not going to go line by line on right vs wrong. I’ll just point out what stood out the most.
Both ruled correctly on the biggest one. Google says 3.6 Flash improves on coding and knowledge work, Artificial Analysis says it does not improve at all, and both models sided with the independent measurement. Both also caught that Google cites Artificial Analysis four times, never once for intelligence.
Like the last test, Opus pulled ahead on facts. It ran the binomial on Anthropic’s eight-of-thirteen claim and found that thirteen coin flips give eight or more heads 29% of the time. It found that Anthropic’s ten-point win came from a 74-task test, small enough that the gap could be luck. Then it noticed the test was version 0.1 and launched the same day as the model, which it called “the fingerprint of an eval developed alongside the model it validates.” Is the monster turning against Frankenstein?
Also like the last test, Fable was slightly stronger when it came to overall reasoning. Fable’s memo ran half the length of Opus’s (I love a rare short AI answer) and was the only one to point out that every independent number in those files came from one company, Artificial Analysis. Its recommendation “is one benchmark-provider failure away from needing a rewrite,” meaning if Artificial Analysis turns out to be wrong or compromised, Fable’s model recommendation becomes inaccurate.
Much to my dismay, both Opus and Fable recommended the same model, Opus 5 (more on that in the key takeaways section). Neither noticed it was an Anthropic model recommending an Anthropic model.
Opus cost $0.79 in 4 minutes 12 seconds and 18.5K output tokens. Fable cost $1.03 in 2 minutes 3 seconds and 9.5K tokens.
It’s hard to judge which was better when neither caught every conflicting claim. After seeing the same pattern in all three tests, I’m confident in saying Fable is better at reasoning, but Opus sees more of the small details. And for now, my job is safe.
Key takeaways
Here are the results and cost chart:
| The metric | Opus 5 | Fable 5 | 
| Bug diagnosis | correct root cause, matches shipped fix | correct root cause, matches shipped fix | 
| Analytics | 26/27, zero false positives | 24/27, zero false positives | 
| Recommendations | 15/16 | 12/16 | 
| Total API time | 23 min 24 s | 24 min 57 s | 
| Total output tokens | 99.9k | 98.3k | 
| Total cost | $6.67 | $11.76 | 
One thing to note before reading that chart. Those counts measure how many items each model found, not how well it thought. Every problem Fable missed was a small, checkable number. Every insight neither model was asked for came from Fable.
Every problem Fable missed was a small, checkable number. Every insight neither model was asked for came from Fable.
Across three tests, the two models produced nearly identical token output volume, 99.9k against 98.3k. Opus’s lower list rates explain much of the cost difference, but billable token mix and model configuration also matter. What I’d love to know (and likely never will) is what makes Opus 5 so much cheaper? Is it the build? Is it purely a play to get people to use Opus 5? Is it part of the AI freemium where it starts cheaper but becomes increasingly more expensive over time?
What do I really think?
For my final thoughts, I’m going to look at the chart above and read between the lines. For best results, use both. And have an expert review the data.
If the job is catching every fact in front of you, use Opus 5. It missed almost nothing across three tests and cost 43% less overall.
Reasoning still hasn’t been perfected when it comes to AI. If the job is catching every fact in front of you, use Opus 5. It missed almost nothing across three tests and cost half as much.
If the job is understanding what the facts add up to, Fable is the clear winner. It was the only model to rebuild the revenue numbers, the only one to explain why the bug was so hard to reproduce, and the only one to name the weakness in its own recommendation.
If the job is understanding what the facts add up to, Fable is the clear winner.
But it still needs work. Fable’s two misses on the spreadsheet were basic, the kind of thing you catch by reading carefully rather than thinking hard. Reasoning can only be so strong if some facts are missing. Fable shows real potential but still needs improvements.

articles.title: What happens when you put AI to work deciphering lost languages?
articles.text:
Every ancient language that has ever been deciphered needed an anchor. Usually that’s a bilingual text, like the Rosetta Stone, or a known relative to compare it to. Linear A, the writing system of the Bronze Age Minoan civilization on the Greek island of Crete, has neither.
Linear A is described as a “language isolate” because it has no confirmed link to any known language, living or dead. As such, it has posed a significant challenge for linguists over the past century.
Etruscan, a language of Italy that was used before the rise of the Roman Empire, has fared only slightly better. A partial vocabulary has been collected from short funerary inscriptions, but its grammar and deeper meaning still elude linguists.
Both languages are exactly the kind of puzzle that AI has recently been pulled into—not by replacing the linguists, but by supercharging their hunches. So does AI actually stand a chance of finishing what a century of human effort hasn’t?
A recent case shows both the appeal and the catch. In June 2026, a self-taught AI engineer and amateur linguist claimed a breakthrough on Linear A. It started from a single guess that one unknown word in a prayer inscription derived from a Semitic root meaning “to dwell” or “to inhabit.”
He then used AI-built programming scripts to test that sound-pattern against the rest of a collected Linear A corpus. He was reportedly able to assign values to 40 signs and compiled a 408-word lexicon, showing—in his view—that Linear A is an extinct member of the Semitic language group, which encompasses languages such as Hebrew and Aramaic.
The need for creativity
It’s worth being precise about what AI did and didn’t do here. It didn’t have the idea. The engineer did.

articles.title: Three US states to deploy 60mph drones armed with pepper spray to neutralize school shooters — ‘Campus Guardian Angel’ drones can also smash windows and ram attackers
articles.text:
Three US states to deploy 60mph drones armed with pepper spray to neutralize school shooters — ‘Campus Guardian Angel’ drones can also smash windows and ram attackers
Anti-shooter system coming to at least three states this year.
The drone arms race is set to enter U.S. schools with Mithril Defense’s Campus Guardian Angel drones in at least nine schools across three states before the year is out. The Washington Post reports that the pilot program will be tested in Florida, Georgia, and Colorado schools with and without resource officers on campus. Securely siloed drones will be situated in key areas around campus, triggered by teachers via app or panic button, then fly to combat gun-toting attackers with a mix of strobes, sirens, pepper spray, and a 60 mph attacker-ramming capability.
If this is a successful initiative, it could go some way to lift the terrible specter of gun violence overshadowing U.S. students. The Washington Post notes that since Columbine in 1999, almost 400,000 students have experienced gun violence at school.
The Campus Guardian Angel drone rollout will be quite expensive. For example, the five schools in Georgia set to adopt drone defense will get $500,000 in backing to run the pilot program. However, politicians and legislators in that state appear to have passed the budget with ease.
This is how the Campus Guardian Angel drone system is designed to work:
- Drones are sited at secure locations around the campus,
- A teacher will trigger the drone deployment using an app or panic button,
- Remote pilots take control and distract, deter, and disable aggressors using a mix of strobes, sirens, pepper gel, and 60‑mph impacts,
- Drone system reaction speed is crucial.
Mithril Defense says that the Campus Guardian Angel drones can react and reach a shooter as quickly as 15 seconds. Justin Marston, Mithril’s founder and CEO, made a few other bold claims regarding his drone system’s reaction speed. For example, Marston said a drone like the Guardian Angel ‘might’ve saved lives in Uvalde.’ That’s a direct reference to the massacre at an elementary school in Uvalde, Texas, where 19 students and two teachers were killed in 2022.
The drone defense firm's CEO underlined that “the first 120 seconds are incredibly critical, because that’s when most of the shooting happens.” That implies that he thinks Campus Guardian Angel drones could be successfully deployed within that very narrow time window. But Uvalde was quite unusual, as responding law enforcement seemed paralyzed, waiting over an hour to enter the classroom.
These school-based drone systems are not without their critics. Some say that the funds may be better spent on prevention than cure. Even Mithril’s founder and CEO’s opinion seems to be that if these drones aren’t prompted into action within two minutes, they aren’t living up to their promise.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
There is also the concern that drones could misidentify students or protection officers when controllers are under pressure. Others say that military-style drone systems aren’t appropriate for schools, and will cost a lot more than simple measures and routines regarding locked doors.
With the three states proceeding with pilot programs this year, we may see the true value and capabilities of the Campus Guardian Angel drones. If these drone-protected schools don’t suffer any terrible shooting incidents, then it may be claimed that the drones are at least a deterrent.
Follow Tom's Hardware on Google News, or add us as a preferred source, to get our latest news, analysis, & reviews in your feeds.
Mark Tyson is a news editor at Tom's Hardware. He enjoys covering the full breadth of PC tech; from business and semiconductor design to products approaching the edge of reason.

articles.title: US-Bundesstaat verbietet KI-Nacktbilder: Warum Elon Musk jetzt dagegen vor Gericht zieht
articles.text:
US-Bundesstaat verbietet KI-Nacktbilder: Warum Elon Musk jetzt dagegen vor Gericht zieht
Das Unternehmen xAI aus Austin im US-Bundesstaat Texas hat rechtliche Schritte gegen den Generalstaatsanwalt von Minnesota, Keith Ellison, eingeleitet. Anlass der Klage ist das als HF 1606 bekannte Gesetz des US-Bundesstaates, das am 1. August 2026 in Kraft treten soll. Dieser Rechtsakt verbietet die Bereitstellung und Nutzung von Software, die Bilder von bekleideten Personen nachträglich durch Künstliche Intelligenz entblößt. Zuwiderhandlungen ziehen massive Strafen nach sich. Bis zu 500.000 US-Dollar werden pro generiertem Bild fällig.
Für die Verantwortlichen bei xAI stellt diese Regelung einen direkten Eingriff in die durch den Ersten Zusatzartikel der US-Verfassung garantierte Meinungsfreiheit dar. Wie aus der offiziellen Klageerhebung vor dem zuständigen US-Bezirksgericht (PDF) hervorgeht, stört sich das von Elon Musk geführte Unternehmen hauptsächlich an der extrem weiten Definition des Begriffs der intimen Körperteile. Der Gesetzgeber soll sich laut xAI bei der Ausarbeitung einer Definition aus dem Sexualstrafrecht bedient haben. Folglich umfasse das Verbot auch die künstliche Generierung von inneren Oberschenkeln, männlichen Brüsten oder Gesäßen.
Die Verfasser der Klageschrift weisen darauf hin, dass eine Plattform mit Millionen aktiven Nutzer:innen schnell eine Summe von 50 Milliarden Dollar an Strafen anhäufen könnte. Das Resultat sei eine juristische Falle. Das Gesetz kriminalisiere harmlose Bilder.
Gefährdungshaftung ohne Ausweg für Plattformbetreiber
Wer künftig humoristische Prompts formuliert und etwa Politiker:innen in Badehosen an einem Strand generiert, löst nach Lesart von xAI bereits einen Verstoß aus. Als konkretes Beispiel führt das Unternehmen ein KI-generiertes Bild an, das den US-Präsidenten Donald Trump sowie weitere Politiker oberkörperfrei im Wasser zeigt.
Die Plattformbetreiber träfe in diesem Szenario eine verschuldensunabhängige Haftung. Strafen greifen selbst dann, wenn Unternehmen strenge Richtlinien durchsetzen und technische Filter tief in die eigenen Systeme integrieren. Ein Haftungsprivileg für „redliche Bemühungen“ existiert in dem Regelwerk nicht. Die Intention der Anwender:innen spielt rechtlich keine Rolle mehr.
Gouverneur Tim Walz unterzeichnete das Gesetz bereits im Vorfeld und ließ über das Netzwerk X in Richtung Elon Musk verlauten: „See you in court, creep“ (etwa: Wir sehen uns vor Gericht, Widerling). Generalstaatsanwalt Keith Ellison schlägt in eine ähnliche Kerbe. Die Nutzung von KI zur Erstellung von Nacktbildern gegen den Willen der Betroffenen ist „erschreckend“, zitiert das lokale Nachrichtenportal MPR News den Generalstaatsanwalt. Es gäbe viele lohnende Debatten über KI, diese gehöre jedoch nicht dazu. Ellison blickt der Klage offensichtlich gelassen entgegen.
Konstruktionsfehler in der Gesetzgebung?
Die Klageschrift verweist ergänzend auf bestehende rechtliche Alternativen. Der US-amerikanische TAKE IT DOWN Act setze beispielsweise zielgerichteter an und definiere illegale Inhalte anatomisch präziser, ohne legitime künstlerische Freiheit zu beschneiden. Dieser Rechtsakt setze zudem eine bewusste Verbreitung der Bilder voraus. Minnesota hingegen bestrafe bereits die rein lokale Generierung auf einem Endgerät, selbst wenn die Datei das System niemals verlässt.
Solche Argumente unterstreichen die Sorge vor einem Overbreadth-Effekt (einer juristischen Überbestimmtheit, die über das eigentliche Regulierungsziel hinausschießt). Das Gesetz verbiete dadurch unbeabsichtigt weite Teile völlig legaler Meinungsäußerung. Das Vorgehen des Parlaments in Minnesota bewerten juristische Beobachter:innen daher durchaus kritisch.
Doch die Argumentation des Unternehmens hat einen Haken: xAI inszeniert sich in der Klageschrift als machtloses Opfer einer überzogenen Regulierung, obwohl das Unternehmen die technischen Werkzeuge für den Missbrauch überhaupt erst programmiert und skaliert. Wer eine Maschine baut, die auf Zuruf extrem realistische Fälschungen menschlicher Körperteile ausgibt, kann die Verantwortung für die absehbaren Konsequenzen nicht vollständig an die Anwenderschaft delegieren. Ein Restzweifel bleibt: Die fortwährende Beteuerung, man sperre ohnehin zehntausende Accounts pro Jahr, belegt letztlich nur, wie unkontrollierbar das eigene Bildgenerierungsmodell in der Praxis tatsächlich agiert. Die eingebauten Filter greifen schlichtweg zu spät oder lassen sich umgehen.
Sollte das Gericht keine einstweilige Verfügung gegen HF 1606 erlassen, kündigte xAI bereits technische Restriktionen an. Das Unternehmen droht damit, die Bildbearbeitungsfunktionen von Grok Imagine für die Anwenderschaft in Minnesota voraussichtlich noch vor dem 1. August 2026 abzuschalten.

articles.title: Spam calls are getting smarter in Canada and here's how Bell is tackling the problem
articles.text:
Spam calls remain a persistent frustration for Canadians, but increasingly sophisticated fraud tactics are making them harder to identify.
One of the fastest-growing challenges is caller ID spoofing — a tactic that manipulates caller ID information to impersonate trusted organizations, local businesses, or personal contacts.
According to the CRTC, roughly 40 per cent of complaints about unwanted calls involve caller ID spoofing and impersonation scams.
As fraud tactics continue to grow more sophisticated, Bell is enhancing its suspicious call detection feature with new capabilities designed to identify, block, and label spoofed calls in real-time — a first for Canadian carriers.
Over 500 million suspicious calls intercepted
So, how does it work? The AI-powered feature analyzes incoming calls in real-time to block or label suspicious calls and help customers make more informed decisions about whether to answer.
Since launching suspicious call detection in May 2025, Bell has blocked or labelled more than 500 million suspicious calls. Approximately 113 million calls have been automatically blocked, while a further 426 million calls have been labelled as “Likely Fraud” or “Possible Spam.”
This has helped identify suspicious activity associated with unknown numbers, but now fraudsters have shifted toward spoofing legitimate phone numbers to appear more credible.
Expanding protection against caller ID spoofing
Beginning in July 2026, suspicious call detection will be enhanced to identify spoofed calls.
Bell is the first carrier in Canada to label and block spoofed calls, allowing these calls to be blocked or labelled using the existing spam and fraud warnings customers already see on their devices.
The company estimates the upgrade will enable suspicious call detection to intercept 60 to 70 per cent more suspicious calls than it currently does.
Even better, no action is required to access the new protection. The enhancement will roll out automatically to all Bell wireless customers on both iOS and Android devices at no additional cost. Bell customers can explore eligible wireless plans and features, including suspicious call detection, on Bell’s rate plans page.
Helping Canada answer with confidence
As phone scams continue to evolve, so must the technologies to stop them.
The latest enhancement reinforces Bell’s continued investment in network security, innovation, and protecting Canadian consumers.
For customers, the benefit is straightforward: additional protection against increasingly sophisticated scam attempts and more information about incoming calls before deciding whether to answer.
More information about Bell’s suspicious call detection feature is available on the Bell website.

articles.title: El Ferrari Luce, diseñado por Jony Ive y odiado por todos, ya vendió lo que tenía previsto para 2026
articles.text:
A dos meses de su polémica presentación, el Ferrari Luce ya cumplió con su objetivo de ventas para todo el año. El primer coche eléctrico de Maranello, diseñado en colaboración con Jony Ive y con un precio de salida de 550.000 euros, vendió lo suficiente como para mantener contentos a los accionistas de la marca.
De acuerdo con el Financial Times, Ferrari estableció una meta de menos de 500 unidades para 2026, la cual se cumplió a principios de julio. Quien más ha tirado del coche ha sido China, donde la demanda por el Luce fue particularmente fuerte desde el principio. Otros que respondieron de forma positiva fueron los emprendedores de Silicon Valley, quienes reservaron el vehículo desde el primer día.
Pese a que el Luce generó una polémica inmediata desde su presentación, lo cierto es que Ferrari no estaba preocupada por satisfacer a sus fanáticos. El fabricante describió su coche eléctrico como una apuesta para conectar con una nueva generación de compradores adinerados que ya están familiarizados con los vehículos eléctricos. Todo apunta a que esa estrategia funcionó mejor de lo esperado y el Luce va encaminado a superar el objetivo para los próximos 4 años.
El lanzamiento del Ferrari Luce ha sido uno de los más complicados para la marca italiana. Tras su anuncio, las redes sociales se llenaron de comentarios que comparaban su diseño con modelos de gama mucho más baja. Luca Cordero di Montezemolo, expresidente de Ferrari, llegó a pedir públicamente que se le retirase el emblema del caballo rampante y aseguró que "al menos este modelo no lo copiarán los chinos".
El Ferrari Luce es uno de los coches eléctricos más controvertidos de los últimos tiempos
Cuando Ferrari encargó el diseño del Luce a LoveFrom, la firma fundada por Jony Ive, muchos anticipaban que el resultado final generaría impacto. No solo por la participación del diseñador del iPhone, sino porque esta era la primera vez que la marca confiaba la responsabilidad a un equipo completamente externo, sin experiencia en diseño automotriz.
El resultado es una carrocería de aluminio con silueta de gota, techo y parabrisas integrados en una sola superficie continua. Con 5,03 metros de longitud y una altura inferior al Purosangue, el Luce rompe con cualquier precedente visual de Maranello, aunque por dentro la diferencia es más evidente. El habitáculo combina aluminio anodizado con pantallas OLED, ofreciendo una experiencia que se acerca más a un dispositivo de Apple que a cualquier otro sistema de infoentretenimiento.
En cuanto a mecánica, el Luce monta cuatro motores eléctricos de imanes permanentes que suman 1.050 CV. El coche puede acelerar de 0 a 100 km/h en 2,5 segundos y alcanza una velocidad máxima superior a los 310 km/h. La batería de 122 kWh cargada a 800 V ofrece más de 530 km de autonomía y admite carga rápida de hasta 350 kW.
La realidad es que ese aspecto "chino" que se le criticaba ha conectado bien con el mercado asiático. A largo plazo, Ferrari aspira a vender unas 2.500 unidades del Luce hasta 2030, lo que equivale a alrededor de 600 coches al año y representa aproximadamente el 5% de sus ventas totales. Benedetto Vigna, CEO de la compañía, dijo que la incursión en el mercado eléctrico no comprometerá el margen operativo del 30% debido a los volúmenes limitados.
Ferrari confirmó que el primer modelo de producción del Luce se subastará el próximo mes y podría superar el millón de dólares.

articles.title: Hint, a new AI startup co-founded by Martha Stewart, offers an AI assistant for homeowners | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Martha Stewart is entering the AI software era in the most Martha Stewart way possible: She has joined the co-founding team at Hint, an app that leverages AI technology to manage the tasks surrounding home maintenance and management. With the Hint app, which launches today, homeowners can tackle challenges around maintenance schedules/tasks and energy management, learn about their soil and air quality, weigh insurance claims, and more.
It can also serve as storage for various contracts, files, and invoices related to the home and its upkeep, which can be queried through the built-in AI assistant.
Co-founder and CTO at Hint, New York-based Kyle Rush, says the home and hospitality empire founder lives nearby and is “very involved” with the startup, but is not a financial investor.
“She’s a real co-founder with a serious stake in equity, and she does work for the company and the app. She’s not a figurehead. I go over about twice a week,” he says. “We sit down and look at the app, and she looks at what it’s saying — when it’s wrong about soil, she’ll say it, and when it’s not right about something about the home…she’ll mention it, and she’ll comment on what I design and the branding and the language. And so she’s, I would say, very involved.”
The startup began in 2024 as a tool to help people navigate decarbonization incentives related to their home, but realized that broadening its use cases had more potential.
“We really quickly realized, why can’t this be the AI for your home? People don’t really have an app to manage their homes…so we just pivoted,” says Rush.
The app joins others in the AI ecosystem that are working to expand AI beyond chatbots to apply the technology to solve real-world problems, while also adding Martha Stewart’s personal expertise to refine the experience.
To get started with Hint, users enter their home address, and the app builds a profile of the home from public data, like property records, weather and soil information, utilities, and more. Users can then upload documents, like inspection reports, home warranties, mortgage documents, contracts, insurance policies, invoices, and more.
This data can tell you things about the soil below the foundation, and how that may affect lawn drainage or foundation risk movement. You can also learn about the air quality surrounding your home or how climate or drought information could impact the potential for floods, your home insurance rates, or your energy usage, among other things.
Then, homeowners upload photos of the home’s major appliances, which allows the app to guide you through any “how to” questions or other maintenance tasks.
This can be surprisingly revealing, as many people don’t know about the smaller tasks related to appliance upkeep.
For instance, you may know to change your refrigerator’s water filter, but did you know that you should occasionally vacuum out the coils on some models to prevent fire hazards? Do you know when to flush a water heater or when to check the salt level for a home well?
Hint’s personalized home maintenance schedule means you won’t have to remember these things, as it sends proactive push notifications about what needs attention and when. This schedule evolves with your home, leveraging its understanding of the house itself, its systems, and the macro environment.
This is where Martha Stewart’s decades of experience in managing homes comes into play, as she’s guided the app development in key areas. In addition, homeowners can use Hint to add one-off tasks to their maintenance plans — like a reminder to replace a damaged window screen or re-caulk some baseboards, or anything else that comes up.
Hint also provides an overall “home score,” offering an at-a-glance number that tells you how good of a job you’re doing managing your home to date.
Meanwhile, Hint’s in-app AI chatbot lets you ask any questions related to your home or your documents. That means you could ask questions as simple as when was the last time you had the AC serviced, or as complex as what you’re paying per kilowatt hour for electricity or whether a HELOC would be a good idea to tap into your home equity.
The app can also guide you through questions related to your homeowner’s insurance, like whether your deductibles are too high, if you’re missing coverage, or whether it makes sense to file a claim for a repair.
Ahead of founding Hint, Rush led engineering at mattress startup Casper during its growth phase and was CTO at online retailer Maisonette. Before that, he built technology for both the Obama and Hillary presidential campaigns. Yih-Han Ma, co-founder and CEO, based out of Charlotte, North Carolina, was previously SVP and GM at Red Ventures, a digital media and technology company.
Rush says the idea for Hint came about as he grew interested in applied AI technology and how it could be put to use for the average homeowner in a more practical way. Under the hood, Hint uses commercial libraries, largely those from OpenAI, as well as Gemini for image work.
The plan is to keep Hint’s AI intelligence free, but later add a premium subscription that could introduce power user features like managing additional properties. The app today generates affiliate revenue from its partner network of service providers, which Rush says is firewalled from the AI so it’s not biased in its recommendations.
Hint (whose name combines the “H” from “home” with “intelligence”) is backed by $10 million in funding from investors, including Montauk Capital, Brian Kelly (The Points Guy), Slow Ventures, Tusk Venture Partners, Energy Impact Partners, Amplo VC, and Hannah Grey.
The iOS app is currently available for free without subscriptions or ads. “We want it to be in the hands of every homeowner in the country,” says Rush.

articles.title: Startup news and updates: daily roundup (June 29, 2026)
articles.text:
Startup news and updates: daily roundup (June 29, 2026)
YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Wednesday, July 29, 2026.
YourStory brings you today’s headlines with the latest developments across sectors.
Featured stories
Inside Magic Bus India Foundation’s Rural Livelihood Programme
Magic Bus India Foundation's Rural Livelihood Programme is designed to help women from economically vulnerable rural households build sustainable livelihoods through entrepreneurship, self-employment, or wage opportunities. Working through a "saturation model," the organisation focuses on selected low-income blocks, partnering with gram panchayats and local stakeholders to identify and enrol women from Below Poverty Line (BPL) families. Participants are assessed for both socio-economic vulnerability and entrepreneurial potential before being introduced to livelihood opportunities based on local market demand.
Funding news
Fixxly raises $5.5M in seed round
Fixxly, a quick commerce startup focused on the building materials sector, has raised $5.5 million in a seed funding round led by Accel, Fireside Ventures, and Lightspeed India Partners.
The fresh capital will be used to strengthen the company's technology platform and scale operations ahead of its commercial launch on September 1. Fixxly will debut in Bengaluru before expanding to other cities.
Founded in 2026 by Shezan Bhojani and Sachith Varma, Fixxly is building a digital procurement platform for the construction and interiors ecosystem. It aims to enable contractors, tradespeople, interior designers, and homeowners to source building materials on demand, with deliveries targeted in about 30 minutes.
Revspot raises $4.8M Series A round
Revspot, an AI-native platform that automates qualified pipeline generation for high-ticket B2C businesses, has raised $4.8 million in a Series A funding round co-led by Inflexor Ventures and Info Edge Ventures.
The round also saw participation from Pentathlon Ventures and Silicon Road Ventures as new institutional investors, along with continued backing from existing investor Titan Capital.
The startup will use the fresh capital to strengthen its product and engineering teams in India, enhance its buyer intelligence and AI-powered lead qualification infrastructure, expand into new high-ticket B2C sectors, and grow its presence in select international markets.
Founded in 2024 by Darshan Subash, Chirag Wadhera, and Varun Garg, Revspot combines AI-driven lead generation and lead qualification into a single platform.
Other news
IIT Madras partners with FaME TN
IIT Madras has partnered with the Bureau for Facilitating MSMEs of Tamil Nadu (FaMe TN), a state government agency, to accelerate digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, and capability building across the state's micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSME) ecosystem.
The initiative will be led by IIT Madras' Center of Tech Excellence with support from a CSR grant by Walmart Global Tech. It aims to digitally empower MSMEs in manufacturing, retail, and allied sectors through technology adoption and capacity-building initiatives.
As part of the collaboration, the partners will develop a State-level MSME Digital Readiness and Adoption Index to assess the digital maturity of enterprises across Tamil Nadu. The programme will also support AI, digital transformation, and Industry 4.0 adoption through digital readiness assessments, training programmes, technology demonstrations, and implementation support.
Emeritus appoints Sachin Mohan as Head of University Partnerships
Global edtech company Emeritus, part of Eruditus, has appointed Sachin Mohan as Head of University Partnerships–India, effective July 2026, as it looks to strengthen collaborations with higher education institutions in one of its key growth markets.
Mohan brings over 15 years of experience in strategic partnerships, business development, P&L management, and enterprise sales across the technology, higher education, and digital sectors in India, Southeast Asia, Australia, the UK, and the US. Most recently, he led global university partnerships at Great Learning, where he worked with leading institutions on executive education, certificate, and degree programmes, while also scaling the company's study abroad business in India. He has previously held leadership roles at Capillary Technologies and Genpact Headstrong Capital Markets.
In his new role, Mohan will lead Emeritus' university partnership strategy in India, working with premier institutions to develop and scale executive education programmes that combine academic excellence with industry relevance.
Data Science Wizards launches AI partnership model for enterprise AI adoption
Data Science Wizards (DSW), the company behind the DSW UnifyAI OS enterprise AI operating system, has launched the DSW AI Partnership Model, a new engagement framework aimed at helping enterprises scale artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilot projects.
The trust-led, long-term framework is designed to help organisations identify high-impact AI use cases, establish governance and technology architecture, deploy AI into production, and continuously optimise outcomes. Built around shared accountability and enterprise ownership, the model seeks to enable businesses to embed AI as a governed, scalable, and sustainable capability rather than a series of fragmented initiatives.
According to the company, the partnership model focuses on delivering measurable business value while helping enterprises build long-term AI capabilities across their operations.
ASMS, ProClime partner to develop biochar-based soil solutions for sustainable agriculture
Avio Smart Market Stack Limited (ASMS) has signed a strategic memorandum of understanding (MoU) with ProClime Services Private Limited to jointly develop and commercialise biochar-based soil enhancement solutions aimed at improving agricultural productivity while supporting India's climate goals.
The partnership combines ASMS' rural distribution network, agricultural expertise, and formulation capabilities with ProClime's expertise in biochar production and carbon project development. Together, the companies will develop scientifically validated biochar-integrated fertiliser formulations designed to improve soil fertility, enhance water retention, boost crop yields, and enable long-term carbon sequestration.
As part of the collaboration, the partners will undertake research, laboratory analysis proposed at IIT Roorkee, field trials, and agronomic validation across multiple crop varieties, soil types, and agro-climatic conditions. They will also evaluate biochar derived from sustainable feedstocks—including bamboo, lantana, senna, pine needles, and agricultural residues—to identify optimal formulations for commercial deployment.
Healthfab signs MoU with Andhra Pradesh govt
FemCare brand Healthfab has announced the signing of an MoU with the Andhra Pradesh Govt to acquire 2 acres of land in Kuppam, Chittoor District to launch its second manufacturing plant for a range of period care panties. The Company plans to invest Rs 15 crore in the unit with an aim to generate over 700 direct and indirect employment.
The expenditure will be spread across factory infrastructure, advanced manufacturing equipment, modern technology, quality assurance infrastructure and workforce development
The proposed manufacturing plant will house Healthfab's vertically integrated manufacturing facility, including production units, quality testing, warehousing, research & development and administrative infrastructure.
With a monthly capacity of over 4 lakh period care panties, the company also plans to design and manufacture reusable period panties, disposable period panties, and other products currently in the pipeline.
CureMeAbroad expands global medical tourism network
Medical tourism startup CureMeAbroad has signed strategic MoUs with Thailand-based Asia Cosmetics and Mexico's Dr. Brenda's Clinic to expand its international healthcare network. The partnerships strengthen the company's presence in two leading medical tourism destinations and improve access for patients from the US, UK, Germany, Australia and GCC countries. Under the agreements, international patients will receive end-to-end support covering treatment planning, travel coordination and post-treatment care. The collaborations also establish a structured framework for patient referrals, quality standards and care coordination, aimed at improving transparency and trust. CureMeAbroad said the expansion comes amid rising global demand for affordable, high-quality cosmetic procedures and will further strengthen its network of verified international healthcare providers.
FNP crosses Rs 1,000 crore revenue, eyes IPO by 2028
Celebrations and gifting platform FNP has crossed Rs 1,000 crore in revenue and is targeting an initial public offering by the end of calendar year 2028, subject to regulatory approvals and market conditions. The company aims to achieve around Rs 1,400 crore in revenue in FY27 and scale to Rs 2,200-2,400 crore before listing. FNP also reported an EBITDA margin of about 3% in FY26, reflecting improved operational efficiency while continuing investments in growth. The company is strengthening its fulfilment network through dark stores, company-operated outlets, central kitchens and cake fulfilment centres to improve delivery speed and customer experience. FNP began by organising India's fragmented flower market before expanding into omnichannel gifting services.
The Standard strengthens India leadership team
US-based insurance and investment company The Standard has announced key leadership appointments for its India operations as it expands strategic capabilities in the country. Operating through centres in Bengaluru and Pune, The Standard India plays a critical role in the company's global technology, digital transformation and operations strategy. The appointments include Atul Agrawal as Head of Technology, Manishekaran Amalasekharan as Head of Finance, Neeti Khanka as Head of Human Resources, Sanjay Pathak as Chief of Staff and India Site Operations Lead, Aditya Pal Singh as Head of Talent Acquisition, Santosh Varier as Head of Administration, and Neeta Sharma as Head of Communications. The company said the appointments will support its long-term growth plans in India.
Ather rolls out AI-powered Pothole+ Alerts
Ather Energy has started rolling out its Pothole+ Alerts feature for Gen 2 and newer scooters, including the 450 Apex, 450X, and Rizta Z. The feature alerts riders to potholes, broken roads, uneven surfaces, and speed breakers ahead using road intelligence generated from data collected by Ather's connected scooter fleet. CEO Tarun Mehta said the technology has been under development for nearly nine years, with the company's growing connected fleet making large-scale road intelligence possible. Alerts are displayed on the scooter dashboard and can also be heard through the Ather Halo smart helmet or compatible Bluetooth headsets. The feature aims to improve rider awareness and road safety through software-driven innovation.
Atlassian adds AI assistant support to Trello
Atlassian has expanded Trello to support the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling AI assistants such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Cursor to manage tasks directly within the platform. Users can create boards, organise cards, update checklists and summarise work using natural language without coding. The feature is available to both free and paid Trello users. Atlassian said users simply need to authorise access by pasting a single URL into a compatible AI assistant before issuing commands. The expansion builds on Atlassian's MCP ecosystem, which has crossed one million monthly active users. The company said the integration will simplify project management by allowing AI assistants to perform actions directly inside Trello.
HPE hosts Code Wars 2026 in Bengaluru
Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) organised its annual Code Wars 2026 competition at its Mahadevapura campus in Bengaluru, bringing together over 300 students from Classes 9 to 12. Participants from Bengaluru, Mysore, Mangaluru, Chennai and Kotagiri competed in coding challenges using C, C++, Java and Python. The event featured more than 20 programming problems designed to test analytical thinking and problem-solving skills while encouraging collaboration and innovation. HPE said Code Wars has become one of India's largest school-level coding competitions and aims to bridge classroom learning with practical application. Winners received advanced technology toolkits and national recognition, while all participants were awarded certificates, prizes and goodies worth Rs 1.5 lakh collectively.
Cloud.in earns AWS Premier Tier status
Hostin Services' cloud transformation business Cloud.in has achieved AWS Premier Tier Services Partner status, the highest level in the AWS Partner Network. The designation recognises partners with strong technical expertise, proven customer success and advanced capabilities in designing, migrating, modernising and managing workloads on Amazon Web Services. Founded in 1999, Hostin Services has over 27 years of experience in enterprise technology infrastructure and has been an AWS Partner since 2014. The company said the recognition reflects its investments in cloud capabilities, certifications and operational excellence. Cloud.in helps enterprises accelerate digital transformation while improving security, governance, resilience, and business agility through AWS-based cloud solutions.
Lemonn posts over 800% revenue growth
Stock broking platform Lemonn, part of the PeepalCo Group, reported more than 800% year-on-year growth in revenue from operations to Rs 8.97 crore in May 2026. Retail trading activity also surged, with order volumes increasing more than ninefold to 27.71 lakh and active traders rising more than fivefold to 24,309. The company said investors from Tier 3 cities accounted for 42.8% of retail orders, followed by Tier 2 cities at 36.7%, highlighting growing participation beyond major urban centres. Since launching in 2024, Lemonn has expanded its offerings across mutual funds, IPO investments and futures and options trading. The company attributed the growth to continuous product innovation and rising adoption among retail investors.
L Catterton appoints Chetan Naik as Managing Director
Global consumer-focused investment firm L Catterton has appointed Chetan Naik as Managing Director to strengthen its India operations. Based in Mumbai, Naik will work with India Executive Chairman Sanjiv Mehta, Partner Vikram Kumaraswamy and the firm's global leadership team to expand its investment platform in the country. Naik joins from 360 ONE Asset, where he led investments across consumer and consumer technology sectors, including beauty, fashion, food delivery, quick commerce and health. Bringing nearly two decades of private equity and venture growth experience, he has supported founders in building category-leading businesses and delivering successful exits. L Catterton said the appointment reinforces its long-term commitment to India's growing consumer market.
(This article will be updated with the latest news throughout the day.)

articles.title: Incendies : Tesla offre la charge gratuite dans 5 Superchargeurs de France
articles.text:
Des feux de forêt d’envergure ravagent une partie du sud de la France. Les canicules à répétition ont abouti à une multiplication d’incendies en Gironde, dans les Landes, le Var, la Corse et les Hautes-Alpes. Alors que la situation se stabilise, en dépit d’une série de reprises de feu, l’empire d’Elon Musk se distingue avec plusieurs mesures d’urgence.
Free Supercharging for France & Spain wildfire relief. Midnight July 29 to midnight August 5 at
Arès, France https://t.co/tUmDPrRaEm
Biganos, France https://t.co/JQzT1kytwf
Mérignac, France https://t.co/mQzt0uZaSQ
Bordeaux Lac, France https://t.co/TEE8ditL13
Bègles, France…— Tesla Charging (@TeslaCharging) July 28, 2026
À lire aussi : Coup dur pour Tesla – la France interdit la conduite autonome et brise le rêve de milliers de conducteurs
Les cinq Superchargeurs Tesla avec recharge gratuite
Tesla vient d’annoncer la mise en place de la recharge gratuite dans cinq Superchargeurs de France. Fort logiquement, il s’agit des stations de recharge qui se trouvent à proximité des sites les plus touchés par les flammes. L’offre est valable pour toutes les voitures qui souhaitent recharger leur batterie dans une station Tesla, même les véhicules d’autres constructeurs. Voici la liste des cinq stations concernées par l’offre d’urgence :
- Arès
- Biganos
- Mérignac
- Bordeaux Lac
- Bègles
L’offre de Tesla ne s’arrête pas aux frontières de l’Hexagone. Le groupe automobile a également activé la recharge gratuite dans les zones d’Espagne touchées par les feux de forêt, à savoir Castellón, Sagunto, Fuenlabrada et Majadahonda. En France comme en Espagne, l’offre est valable jusqu’au 5 août 2026.
@elonmusk Two major wildfires are forcing evacuations in southwest France today. Thousands of EVs are on the roads. Could @Tesla temporarily offer free Supercharging in the affected region to help evacuees? Every bit of support matters. 🙏🇫🇷 pic.twitter.com/0jL5UiXxDm
— Tesla Owners Club France (@TeslaClubFrance) July 25, 2026
L’idée ne vient pas de nulle part. Quelques jours plus tôt, le Tesla Owners Club France, qui se présente comme « le club officiel pour les propriétaires » de Tesla du pays, a interpellé la marque sur le réseau social X. Le club avait demandé à Tesla de « proposer temporairement la recharge gratuite aux Superchargeurs dans la région sinistrée pour aider les personnes évacuées ».
En parallèle, Starlink, une autre entreprise de l’empire d’Elon Musk, a proposé son aide à la France. La filiale de SpaceX s’est dite prête à activer gratuitement en France son service satellite d’urgence Direct-to-Cell. Ce dispositif permettrait aux smartphones compatibles de basculer automatiquement sur le réseau satellitaire si les réseaux terrestres deviennent indisponibles. La société attend encore le feu vert des autorités françaises, qui n’ont pas réagi à ce stade.

articles.title: La franchise Resident Evil dépasse Final Fantasy avec 213 millions de jeux vendus
articles.text:
Capcom vient tout juste de mettre à jour les chiffres de ses différentes marques et on imagine que le champagne a dû être réservé au frais. Sa saga Resident Evil, qui existe depuis des dizaines et des dizaines d’années, pèse désormais 213 millions de ventes selon le bilan financier publié le 28 juillet 2026.
Resident Evil fait donc mieux que Final Fantasy, dont les derniers chiffres, partagés en juin 2026, font état de 212 millions de ventes dans le monde. Les volumes sont assez proches, mais la victoire reste symbolique pour Capcom, qui installe Resident Evil tout en haut du classement des marques japonaises les plus puissantes (hors Nintendo et Pokémon).
Resident Evil > Final Fantasy (pour un million de ventes)
Dans le détail, le remake de Resident Evil 2 est désormais l’opus le plus vendu de la saga, avec 19,75 millions de ventes, devant Resident Evil 5 (19,01 millions) et Resident Evil 7: Biohazard (18,41 millions). Il sera a priori bientôt dépassé par un autre remake : celui de Resident Evil 4, qui en est déjà à 16,04 millions d’unités écoulées et a le momentum pour lui (2,43 millions de ventes sur le dernier trimestre, contre 1,42 million pour Resident Evil 2). Sorti cette année, Resident Evil Requiem en est déjà à 8,06 millions de ventes.
Pour en revenir à la comparaison entre Resident Evil et Final Fantasy, il est nécessaire de prendre en compte le nombre de jeux sortis. En comptant les jeux majeurs, les spin-off, les remakes, les remasterisations, les dérivés annexes (mobiles, arcades…), on dépasse la soixantaine de jeux pour l’un, et la centaine pour l’autre. Notons que, sur la série principale, on est à seize opus pour Final Fantasy et dix pour Resident Evil (de zéro à neuf, sans compter les remakes). Il faut par ailleurs garder en mémoire que Final Fantasy date de 1987, quand le tout premier Resident Evil est sorti en 1996. N’oublions pas non plus que Square Enix a eu une politique davantage tournée vers les exclusivités temporaires ces dernières années, ce qui limite mécaniquement son volume de ventes.
À noter quand même que les licences Resident Evil et Final Fantasy se sont moins vendues que le seul GTA 5, qui a franchi la barre des 230 millions de copies écoulées selon le dernier bilan financier de Take-Two Interactive (partagé en mai). Cela rappelle à quel point le titre de blockbuster est une véritable anomalie statistique. Et on s’attend à un destin similaire avec GTA 6, disponible en précommande depuis le mois de juin.

articles.title: Tineco Floor One S7 Pro : 50 € de remise sur Amazon
articles.text:
Le Tineco Floor One S7 Pro s'attaque à la corvée du nettoyage des sols durs en combinant aspiration et lavage humide dans un seul appareil sans fil. Grâce à sa technologie SmoothPower et son éclairage LED intégré, il promet un entretien plus efficace tout en repérant automatiquement les saletés invisibles à l'œil nu.
Le Floor One S7 Pro appartient à la gamme haut de gamme des aspirateurs-laveurs Tineco, pensée pour remplacer le duo classique aspirateur et serpillière en un seul geste. Il embarque le capteur intelligent iLoop, capable d'ajuster automatiquement la puissance d'aspiration et le débit d'eau selon le niveau de salissure détecté sur le sol. articles.title: Mate Security Raises $35 Million for Agentic SOC
articles.text:
AI-powered Security Operations Center (SOC) startup Mate Security has announced raising $35 million in a Series A funding round that brings the total raised by the company to over $50 million.
Led by Canaan Partners, with additional support from Insight Partners, Microsoft’s Venture Fund M12, and Team8, the investment round comes eight months after the company emerged from stealth mode.
Founded in 2025 by former Wiz and Microsoft veterans, Tel Aviv-based Mate has built an open, agentic platform that relies on AI to transform security operations into continuously learning defense systems.
Mate’s agentic SOC creates a unique security context graph for each organization, based on assets, business processes, users, and data, which is then used to build detections, triage and investigate incidents, and perform threat hunting and incident response.
By using unique context graphs, Mate’s agents operate within each organization’s context to provide tailored, up-to-date defenses.
They operate in a Continuous Detection, Continuous Response (CDCR) framework, retaining knowledge with each investigation to improve detections that feed the next investigation.
Planning to double its workforce by the end of the year, Mate will use the fresh investment to expand its customer support, sales, and R&D teams, as well as its market presence.
“When we started Mate, we knew we had to invest in the foundation: context and trust, and build them deeply into our product. We will continue moving fast and stay laser-focused on our customers, as we expand into new markets and categories to build the Open Security Operations foundation of the future,” said Mate co-founder and CEO Asaf Wiener.

articles.title: Incendies de Gironde : la photo en Une du New York Times sort d'un vieil Android
articles.text:
Un couple installé sous un parasol orange, deux transats rayés, une planche de bodyboard oubliée dans le sable. Devant eux, en arrière-plan, une colonne de fumée qui avale l’horizon et teinte le ciel d’orange. La scène a été captée le 24 juillet 2026 sur la plage du Moutchic, au bord du lac de Lacanau, en Gironde. En quelques heures, elle est passée des réseaux sociaux aux Unes de la presse internationale.
Derrière l’appareil, Maximilien Lamy, éditeur photo à l’AFP depuis plus de vingt ans. Il n’était pas missionné : il passait ses vacances sur place avec sa compagne et sa fille, et s’est garé un peu trop loin du restaurant, ce qui l’a fait longer la plage à pied comme il le raconte dans une interview.
En face, l’incendie de Saumos ravageait la rive du lac, un feu que l’AFP compte parmi les plus dévastateurs pour les forêts françaises depuis 1945. Plus de 200 000 personnes ont été évacuées dans le Sud-Ouest ce week-end-là, et des cartes comme Flamap permettaient d’en suivre l’avancée quasiment en temps réel.
L’image sort quasiment brute du téléphone. Elle a juste été recadrée sur les côtés, sans autre modification, a expliqué le photographe.
Le HONOR Magic V6 repousse les limites du smartphone pliable avec un design distinctif et robuste, des performances photo de haut niveau et une batterie généreuse conçue pour durer.
Franchement, le rendu est tel que certains internautes ont d’abord cru à une image générée par intelligence artificielle. Maximilien Lamy, lui, résume la prise de vue sans emphase : « j’ai juste vu la composition, j’ai saisi le contraste ».
Un vieux smartphone Android, et pas question de dire lequel
Quel modèle ? Mystère. Maximilien Lamy n’a pas voulu communiquer la marque, et l’AFP nous l’a confirmé : c’est un choix assumé, pour ne pas offrir de publicité gratuite au constructeur. Le téléphone est un « Android assez ancien, mais un bon photophone auquel le photographe tient », nous souffle son agent. L’appareil a déjà quelques années au compteur.
À retenir, cette phrase qu’il glisse dans la vidéo publiée par l’AFP : « le meilleur appareil photo, c’est celui qu’on a toujours sur soi ». La formule n’est pas de lui : elle a été popularisée par le photographe américain Chase Jarvis, qui en a fait le titre d’un livre en 2009 consacré à ses images prises à l’iPhone.
    Pour aller plus loin
            Les meilleurs smartphones photo en 2026, comparatif et tests des photophones
            
Sur le papier, un photophone haut de gamme comme le Xiaomi 15 Ultra ou un compact expert du genre du Canon EOS R50 écrasent n’importe quel vieux téléphone. Sauf que la meilleure image reste celle qu’on peut réellement déclencher au bon moment, et là, c’était un smartphone au fond d’une poche.
On a fouillé le fichier pour retrouver le modèle
Puisque la marque restait secrète, on a cherché dans le fichier lui-même. Une photo transporte en principe des métadonnées EXIF, ces informations que l’appareil inscrit au déclenchement : marque, modèle, ouverture, sensibilité, parfois la position GPS. Les smartphones ont beau avoir rattrapé une bonne partie du terrain en photo, ces traces restent normalement présentes. Sauf que dans le fichier acquis auprès de l’agence, il n’y a plus rien : aucun bloc EXIF, aucune donnée XMP, l’autre grand format de métadonnées.
    À lire aussi : 
    Comment supprimer les métadonnées EXIF de vos photos
Ce qui subsiste, c’est un profil colorimétrique, un marqueur d’encodage et une fiche IPTC, la petite étiquette de légende, de crédit et de lieu réécrite par le logiciel qui prépare les images pour la diffusion.
Le fichier a été enregistré en dernier par un logiciel Adobe à qualité maximale, signe qu’un poste de retouche sur ordinateur est passé par là après le téléphone. Restait un indice, le profil colorimétrique embarqué, un Display P3 signé Apple, autrement dit une palette de couleurs propre à la marque. De quoi conclure à un iPhone ? On l’a cru un moment.
Sauf qu’en comparant ce profil octet par octet (via exiftool) à celui qu’écrit un iPhone récent, ça ne colle pas : le fichier de l’agence porte la révision de 2015, quand les iPhone à jour embarquent celle de 2022.
L’AFP a fini par trancher, et la réponse invalide toute la piste : la photo a bien été prise avec un smartphone Android. Le profil Apple ne venait pas du téléphone, mais d’un ordinateur intervenu plus loin dans la chaîne. Sûrement l’ordinateur de la retoucheuse, Maelle Lions-Geollot.
La leçon est finalement assez simple. La photo la plus vue de cet été de feux a été prise avec un vieil Android glissé dans une poche de vacances, un appareil déjà daté que son propriétaire trouve encore bon en photo. Pour l’immense majorité des situations, un photophone d’il y a quelques années suffit largement ; le reste tient à l’œil du photographe et au fait d’être là au bon moment.
